\mxunit{automatismes-ch12}{Probability: conditioning and weighted trees}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Tue~4~May~2027}{Probability model and equally likely outcomes}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{A fair coin is tossed three times. How many outcomes are there?}{$2^3=8$ equally likely outcomes.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{Biased die: $P(6)=\num{0,25}$ and the other five faces are equally likely. Calculate $P(1)$.}{$\dfrac{1-\num{0,25}}{5}=\num{0,15}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · Critical thinking}{PRB}{``It will rain or it will not rain tomorrow: so there is a one in two chance.'' Is this equally-likely model justified?}{No: having two outcomes does not make them equally likely. Equal likelihood is an assumption of the model that must be justified.}{}
\mxfq{Review · Quick}{PER}{Which shapes make up the net of a square-based pyramid?}{$1$ square and $4$ (isosceles) triangles.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Translate}{LIT}{Each side of a square of side $x$ is increased by $3$. Express the increase in area in terms of $x$.}{$(x+3)^2-x^2=6x+9$.}{}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Mon~10~May~2027}{Law of large numbers (informal version): simulation}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{STA}{In $100$ tosses, $47$ are ``heads''. What is the relative frequency of ``heads''?}{$\num{0,47}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Interpret}{PRB}{Why, in $10$ tosses of a fair coin, can the frequency of ``heads'' stray from $\num{0,5}$? What happens with $\num{10000}$ tosses?}{Sampling fluctuation: a small sample has high variability. For large samples, the frequency stabilises near the probability $\num{0,5}$ (law of large numbers).}{}
\mxfq{Core + · True/false}{PRB}{True or false? Justify. Tossing a fair coin $\num{1000}$ times gives exactly $500$ ``heads''.}{False. The number obtained is close to $500$, rarely exactly $500$.}{}
\mxfq{Review · Problem}{MOD}{Price including tax $P(x)=\num{1,2}\,x$ ($\pc{20}$ VAT). Calculate $P(250)$ and the preimage of $480$.}{$P(250)=300$; $\num{1,2}x=480\Leftrightarrow x=400$.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Method}{EQ}{Solve in $\R$: $\dfrac{2x-1}{3}=\dfrac{x+4}{2}$.}{$x=14$}{Cross-multiplication: $2(2x-1)=3(x+4)$.}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Tue~11~May~2027}{Python simulation of a repeated random experiment}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{$P(A)=\num{0,35}$. Calculate $P(\overline A)$.}{$1-\num{0,35}=\num{0,65}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Reading code}{ALG}{What does this program compute? Roughly what value will it display?\mxpseudo{from random import randint\\ compte = 0\\ for i in range(1000):\\ \mxtab if randint(1, 6) == 6:\\ \mxtab\mxtab compte = compte + 1\\ print(compte / 1000)}}{The frequency of a $6$ in $\num{1000}$ rolls of a die; about $\dfrac16\approx\num{0,167}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · Method}{PRB}{Fair $12$-sided die with faces numbered $1$ to $12$. Probability of getting a prime number?}{Primes: $2\,;\,3\,;\,5\,;\,7\,;\,11$: $\dfrac{5}{12}$ ($1$ is not prime).}{}
\mxfq{Review · Construction}{CON}{$M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $[AB]$. What can be said about $MA$ and $MB$? How is it constructed with compasses?}{$MA=MB$. Construction: two arcs of the same radius (greater than $\frac12AB$) centred at $A$ and $B$; their intersections define the perpendicular bisector.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Recognise}{SOL}{What is the shape of the cross-section of a cube by a plane parallel to one of its faces?}{A square with the same side as the face.}{}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Thu~13~May~2027}{Conditional probability $P_A(B)$}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{Among $25$ canteen users, $15$ are girls. A canteen user is chosen at random: probability that this is a girl?}{$\dfrac{15}{25}=\num{0,6}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{In a class of $30$ pupils, $12$ play football, of whom $5$ also play handball. A pupil is chosen at random: calculate $P_F(H)$, where $F$: ``plays football'', $H$: ``plays handball''.}{$P_F(H)=\dfrac{\Card(F\cap H)}{\Card(F)}=\dfrac5{12}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · Method}{PRB}{In an equally likely model, $\Card(A)=50$ and $\Card(A\cap B)=20$. Calculate $P_A(B)$.}{$\dfrac{20}{50}=\num{0,4}$.}{}
\mxfq{Review · Quick}{NUM}{Put in increasing order: $\dfrac74$, $-\dfrac32$, $\num{0,5}$.}{$-\dfrac32<\num{0,5}<\dfrac74$ ($-\num{1,5}<\num{0,5}<\num{1,75}$).}{}
\mxfq{Thread · True/false}{DEM}{True or false? Justify. A quadrilateral with two opposite sides parallel is a parallelogram.}{False. Counter-example: a trapezium (not a parallelogram) has only one pair of parallel sides.}{}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Tue~18~May~2027}{Conditional probability and two-way tables}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{In the following table, what is the total of the ``sport'' row?\par\smallskip\mxarraystretch{1.15}\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline
 & Girls & Boys & Total \\ \hline
Sport & 18 & 22 & \ldots \\ \hline
No sport & 12 & 8 & 20 \\ \hline
Total & 30 & 30 & 60 \\ \hline
\end{tabular}\par }{$18+22=40$.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{A pupil is chosen at random from this table. Calculate $P(S)$, $P_F(S)$ and $P_S(F)$ ($F$: girl, $S$: does sport).}{$P(S)=\dfrac{40}{60}=\dfrac23$; $P_F(S)=\dfrac{18}{30}=\num{0,6}$; $P_S(F)=\dfrac{18}{40}=\num{0,45}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · True/false}{PRB}{True or false? Justify. In this table, $P_F(S)=P_S(F)$.}{False. $\num{0,6}\neq\num{0,45}$: the reference sets ($30$ girls and $40$ sports participants) differ.}{}
\mxfq{Review · Quick}{PUI}{Calculate $5^0+2^{-1}$.}{$1+\dfrac12=\dfrac32$.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Method}{REP}{$ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $A\pt{1;1}$, $B\pt{5;2}$, $C\pt{6;5}$. Find $D$.}{The diagonals have the same midpoint: $D=A+C-B=\pt{2;4}$. Check: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}=\pt{4;1}$.}{}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Thu~20~May~2027}{Weighted trees: construction}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{What is the sum of the probabilities of the branches leaving a single node?}{$1$.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{In a population, $\pc{30}$ have a disease $M$. A test is positive ($T$) for $\pc{90}$ of those with the disease and for $\pc{5}$ of those without it. Complete the branch probabilities of the tree.}{$P(M)=\num{0,3}$, $P(\overline M)=\num{0,7}$; $P_M(T)=\num{0,9}$, $P_M(\overline T)=\num{0,1}$; $P_{\overline M}(T)=\num{0,05}$, $P_{\overline M}(\overline T)=\num{0,95}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · Translate}{PRB}{Translate into symbols: ``among those with the disease, $\pc{90}$ test positive''.}{$P_M(T)=\num{0,9}$: branch $M\to T$; do not write $P(T)=\num{0,9}$.}{}
\mxfq{Review · Quick}{CAL}{Calculate $\dfrac23\div\dfrac49$.}{$\dfrac23\times\dfrac94=\dfrac{18}{12}=\dfrac32$.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Problem}{DIV}{Three lighthouses flash every $6$, $8$ and $9$ seconds. They light up together at $t=0$. When is the next simultaneous flash?}{$\ppcm\pt{6;8;9}=72$: after $72$ s.}{}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Mon~24~May~2027}{Weighted trees: multiplying along a path}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{CAL}{Calculate $\num{0,3}\times\num{0,9}$.}{$\num{0,27}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{Using the tree from sheet 70, calculate $P(M\cap T)$ and $P(\overline M\cap T)$.}{$P(M\cap T)=\num{0,3}\times\num{0,9}=\num{0,27}$; $P(\overline M\cap T)=\num{0,7}\times\num{0,05}=\num{0,035}$.}{We multiply along a path: $P(M\cap T)=P(M)\times P_M(T)$.}
\mxfq{Core + · Method}{PRB}{Deduce $P(T)$.}{Two paths lead to $T$: $\num{0,27}+\num{0,035}=\num{0,305}$.}{}
\mxfq{Review · Factorise}{DEV}{Factorise $x^2-9$.}{$(x-3)(x+3)$.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Quick}{GEO}{The side $[BC]$ of length $13$ cm is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle $ABC$. What is the radius of its circumscribed circle?}{The midpoint of the hypotenuse is the centre: radius $=13\div2=\num{6,5}$ cm.}{}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Tue~25~May~2027}{From table to tree and symbolic notation}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{Express $\dfrac{30}{60}$ as a probability.}{$\num{0,5}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{From the table on sheet 69, build the tree ($F$ or $G$, then $S$ or $\overline S$): give $P(F)$, $P_F(S)$ and $P_G(S)$.}{$P(F)=\num{0,5}$; $P_F(S)=\dfrac{18}{30}=\num{0,6}$; $P_G(S)=\dfrac{22}{30}=\dfrac{11}{15}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · Translate}{PRB}{Write symbolically and calculate ``the probability of being a boy who does not do sport''.}{$P(G\cap\overline S)=\dfrac{8}{60}=\dfrac{2}{15}$; or $\num{0,5}\times\dfrac{8}{30}$.}{}
\mxfq{Review · Quick}{QP}{A car travels at constant speed: $150$ km in $2$ h. What distance in $5$ h?}{$75\times5=375$ km.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Statement → formula}{REG}{A taxi charges a pick-up fee of $\num{2000}$ Ar then $\num{1500}$ Ar per km. Express the price $p(x)$ for $x$ km, then calculate $p(8)$.}{$p(x)=\num{1500}x+\num{2000}$; $p(8)=\num{14000}$ Ar.}{}
\end{fluencysheet}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Thu~27~May~2027}{Reversing conditioning: $P_A(B)$ and $P_B(A)$}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{What is the difference between $P_M(T)$ and $P_T(M)$?}{$P_M(T)$: probability of testing positive given that one has the disease; $P_T(M)$: of having the disease given that one tests positive.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{Using the data from sheet 70 ($P(M\cap T)=\num{0,27}$ and $P(T)=\num{0,305}$), calculate $P_T(M)$.}{$P_T(M)=\dfrac{P(M\cap T)}{P(T)}=\dfrac{\num{0,27}}{\num{0,305}}\approx\num{0,885}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · Method}{PRB}{Rare disease ($\pc{1}$ of the population); the test is positive for $\pc{99}$ of those with the disease and $\pc{5}$ of those without. Calculate $P_T(M)$.}{$P(M\cap T)=\num{0,0099}$; $P(\overline M\cap T)=\num{0,99}\times\num{0,05}=\num{0,0495}$; $P(T)=\num{0,0594}$; $P_T(M)=\dfrac{\num{0,0099}}{\num{0,0594}}=\dfrac16\approx\num{0,17}$.}{Counter-intuitive result: a test that is ``$\pc{99}$ reliable'' is not enough.}

\begin{fluencysheet}{Mon~31~May~2027}{False positives and false negatives}
\mxfq{Warm-up · Quick}{PRB}{Define ``false positive'' and ``false negative''.}{False positive: positive test for a person who does not have the disease. False negative: negative test for a person who has the disease.}{}
\mxfq{Core · Method}{PRB}{$\num{10000}$ people, $\pc{2}$ with the disease; the test is positive for $\pc{90}$ of those with the disease and $\pc{10}$ of those without. How many false negatives, false positives and positives in total?}{With the disease $200$: $180$ positive, so $20$ false negatives; without the disease $\num{9800}$: $980$ false positives; positives: $180+980=\num{1160}$.}{}
\mxfq{Core + · Interpret}{PRB}{Using the previous data, calculate the proportion of people who truly have the disease among the positives and comment.}{$\dfrac{180}{\num{1160}}\approx\pc{15,5}$: since the disease is rare, most positives are false positives.}{}
\mxfq{Review · True/false}{PNP}{True or false? Justify. The area of a square is proportional to the length of its side.}{False. $c=1\mapsto1$ and $c=2\mapsto4\neq2\times1$.}{}
\mxfq{Thread · Disprove}{LIT}{Conjecture: ``for every integer $n$, $n^2+n+41$ is prime''. Test $n=40$.}{$40^2+40+41=1681=41^2$: not prime. The conjecture is false.}{Successful tests prove nothing; one failed test disproves.}
